title: The moon outshines
hookLine: all merit-making is not worth a sixteenth part of metta, as starlight to moonlight

cards: Go outside on a clear night far from city lights, and the stars are astonishing, the whole sky crowded. Then the full moon rises. As it climbs, the fainter stars fade out.
They're all still there. The moon just outshines them. The Itivuttaka uses that exact sight.
Yesterday it praised giving as something people would never skip if they understood it. Right after, it says there's something brighter still.

teach.h: NOT A SIXTEENTH PART OF METTA.
teach.b: Whatever grounds there are for making merit, the Buddha says, giving, offerings, good works of every kind, all of them together are not worth a sixteenth part of the mind's release through metta, loving-kindness.
Metta outshines them; it shines and glows and blazes. Then three pictures.
As the light of all the stars together is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon's light.
As in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the sky is clear, the sun rising into the sky drives away all the darkness.

teach.h: THE AUTUMN SUN, THE MORNING STAR.
teach.b: As at the end of the night, the morning star shines and glows and blazes. Not worth a sixteenth part: a tiny fraction. Notice what's being compared.

Giving is good; yesterday's teaching made that clear, and nothing here takes it back. But giving is something you do. Metta, here, is something you become: a mind that wishes well to every being, without measure.

teach.h: THE GIFT AND THE HEART IT COMES FROM.
teach.b: One way to hear it: the gift is one star, and the heart it comes from is the moon.

And the verse at the end: one who develops metta has their fetters wear thin. Even toward one being, loving-kindness makes a person good. Toward all beings, with a kind heart, the noble one makes abundant merit.

how: Metta practice is taught in Theravada communities and in other Buddhist schools; practitioners often begin with someone easy to love and widen the wish of goodwill step by step to all beings.

o: a gift of food to the monks

s: it says all merit-making is not worth a sixteenth of metta; it doesn't take back the praise of giving.
the teaching compares metta to the moon among the stars
the light of all the stars is not a sixteenth of the moon's.
the teaching uses three pictures of light
the moon among the stars, the autumn sun, and the morning star.

games.q: you've given generously all year. you ask what could possibly be worth more. what does Itivuttaka 27 say?
games.why: all grounds for merit together aren't worth a sixteenth part of metta, as the stars aren't worth a sixteenth of the moon.

practice: Start with one being who is easy to love, a child, a friend, a pet, and wish them well: may you be well, may you be happy.

Then let it widen, to the people in this building, this street, this city, and wider, without forcing; the moon doesn't strain to shine. When the mind wanders, come back to that first easy face, and begin again.

wordCard.voice: Metta, loving-kindness. Itivuttaka 27: all merit-making together is not worth a sixteenth part of this, as starlight is to the moon. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali metta: loving-kindness, goodwill. Itivuttaka 27 praises metta cetovimutti, the mind's release through metta.

carryVoice: Your line: let goodwill rise first. Giving shines; metta, the text says, shines brighter. That's day six hundred twenty-nine.
